title: Enterocutaneous Fistula
subject: Surgery
summary: An enterocutaneous fistula (ECF) is an abnormal tract between the gastrointestinal lumen and skin, causing loss of fluid, electrolytes, and nutrients. Management focuses on source control, nutrition, and sepsis prevention, with higher mortality in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: An ECF is a pathological communication that allows intestinal contents to exit through the skin. Diagnosis is clinical: visible external opening with stool or bilious drainage, confirmed by contrast study if needed.
b: External opening with enteric output
Surrounding skin irritation or maceration
Fistula output measured in mL/24 h

sections.p: The most widely used classification is based on output volume and anatomical location, which predicts nutritional loss and mortality risk.
b: Low output: <200 mL/24 h (usually distal colon)
Moderate output: 200‑500 mL/24 h
High output: >500 mL/24 h (proximal small bowel)
Proximal location and high output carry highest mortality

sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, postoperative leaks dominate, but infectious and inflammatory conditions are also common.
b: Post‑operative anastomotic leak (most common)
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn’s, ulcerative colitis)
Abdominal tuberculosis or perforated typhoid
Radiation enteritis
Trauma or penetrating injury
Neoplasia with tumor erosion
Herbal or traditional remedies causing ulceration

sections.p: Patients often present with a draining wound, abdominal pain, and systemic signs of fluid loss or infection.
b: Visible stool, bile, or serous fluid from skin
Peri‑fistular skin maceration, erythema, or ulceration
Fever, tachycardia, hypotension if sepsis
Dehydration, weight loss, electrolyte abnormalities

t.b: What is the anatomy of the tract? – Shows origin, course, and distal obstruction.
Is the patient malnourished or septic? – Low albumin/↑CRP suggest poor nutrition and inflammation.
Is there an intra‑abdominal collection? – Detects abscess or fluid collection.
What is the output volume? – Guides classification and nutrition plan.
Does immunosuppression contribute? – Positive result may affect healing and infection risk.

sections.p: Complications drive mortality and dictate urgent action.
b: Sepsis with hypotension or organ dysfunction
High‑output (>500 mL/24 h) leading to acute renal failure
Electrolyte derangements (hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis)
Skin necrosis or massive hemorrhage from the tract
Abdominal compartment syndrome

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, control output, replace fluids/nutrients, and prevent infection.
b: Source control: surgical repair or percutaneous drainage if sepsis
Broad‑spectrum antibiotics covering gram‑negative and anaerobes (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam, metronidazole) – avoid nephrotoxic agents in renal failure
Fluid replacement: replace losses 1‑1.5 × measured output; add potassium as needed
Enteral nutrition if distal gut usable; otherwise, parenteral nutrition for high‑output or proximal fistulas
Skin protection: barrier dressings, frequent change, topical antiseptics
Avoid nasogastric suction in high‑output proximal fistulas – worsens loss

sections.p: Long‑term care aims to close the fistula and restore nutrition.
b: Weekly output measurement and wound assessment
Nutritional labs every 1‑2 weeks
Optimize glycemic control, treat anemia, and manage HIV/TB if present
Elective definitive surgery after sepsis control and nutritional repletion (usually >6 weeks)
Educate patients on wound care and signs of infection
Entero‑atmospheric fistula – open abdomen without overlying skin
Entero‑enteric fistula – internal bowel‑to‑bowel connection
Cutaneous abscess with feculent discharge – no true tract
Normal CRP early in sepsis – may be falsely low in immunocompromised patients
Serum albumin low for chronic disease, not acute loss – does not reflect current fluid status
Ultrasound may miss a deep fistulous tract – consider CT or fistulogram if suspicion remains

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden increase in output >500 mL/24 h with hypotension
Rapid skin breakdown or massive bleeding from the tract

faq.q: Why is high output more dangerous than low output?
faq.a: High output causes greater fluid, electrolyte, and nutrient loss, leading quickly to dehydration, renal failure, and malnutrition.

faq.q: Can an ECF close on its own?
faq.a: Spontaneous closure occurs in <30 % of low‑output, distal fistulas when infection is controlled and nutrition is adequate.
When sepsis persists despite drainage, the fistula is high‑output with proximal origin, or after 6 weeks of optimal medical therapy without closure.

exam: What bedside findings differentiate a high‑output proximal ECF from a low‑output distal one? — Measure 24‑h output, note stool characteristics, and locate the opening relative to the umbilicus.

A patient with a postoperative ECF has a serum albumin of 2.5 g/dL but normal CRP. How do you interpret this? — Low albumin reflects chronic loss; normal CRP does not exclude early sepsis, so monitor closely.

Why is total parenteral nutrition preferred over enteral feeding in a high‑output jejunal fistula? — Enteral feeds increase fistula output and risk of electrolyte loss; TPN bypasses the gut and allows healing.

Which antibiotic regimen is appropriate for an ECF in a setting with high rates of anaerobic infection and limited drug formulary? — Ampicillin‑sulbactam plus metronidazole covers gram‑negatives and anaerobes without needing expensive carbapenems.

A patient’s fistula output suddenly rises to 800 mL/24 h with new fever. What is your next step? — Assume sepsis; obtain cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and assess for intra‑abdominal collection needing drainage.
How does HIV infection affect the prognosis of an ECF? — Immunosuppression delays healing, increases infection risk, and may require earlier surgical intervention.
When is a fistulogram preferred over CT in low‑resource hospitals? — When CT is unavailable or contraindicated; contrast study directly visualises the tract and distal patency.
What skin care measures reduce morbidity around an ECF? — Use barrier creams, sterile dressings, and change dressings every 24 h to prevent maceration and secondary infection.
